blocks.text: The thymus
INTRODUCTION
The thymus is a large odd and medial primary (central) epithelial organ located in the upper part of the anterior mediastinum.
-10 to 15 g at birth, 30 to 40 g at puberty then progressive involution
-Consisted of two lobes divided into incomplete lobules
-Organ where immature (prothymocytes) and naive T lymphocytes from the bone marrow differentiate into mature lymphocytes.
Embryological reminder
The thymus has a dual origin: entoblastic and mesenchymal
Endoderm entoblast epithelial reticular cells of the thymus framework
Extra embryonic mesoderm mesenchyme pluripotent stem cell at the origin of hematopoietic cells including lymphocytes
The thymus
develops around the 5th week from the 3rd and 4th entoblast pocket.
The thymic outline

is penetrated by the mesenchyme of the branchial arches which incompletely subdivides it into lobes and lobules and provides blood vessels and also receives neural crest cells from the cephalic region.
Thymus lymphocytes are of mesenchymal origin, originating in the marrow and undergoing their differentiation in the thymus.
Structure
In young subjects, the thymus is made up of two lobes
Each lobe presents to be described:
- A connective capsule
-a cortex
-a spinal cord

blocks.text: the lobule is,
Surrounded by a thin connective capsule, it contains:
-a dark peripheral or cortical zone cut by the intralobular trabeculae into nodules
-a central clear or medullary region, common to all nodules and containing particular formations: the HASSAL corpuscles.
All of the lobules form the 2 anatomical lobes of the thymus.
Overview of a thymus (MO-HES)
1-capsule, 2-interlobular septum; 3-cortex; 4-medullary
Overview of a thymus (MO-HES)
1-capsule, 2-interlobular septum; 3-cortex; 4-medullary
Child's thymus; overview

Its structure is lobulated. In each lobule there is a dark cortex and a pale medulla. The thymus does not contain any rounded nodules or germinal centers in the cortex, the lymphocytes are arranged in a diffuse mass.
Adult thymus. Overview
The parenchyma is largely replaced by adipose tissue. We can recognize remains of the lymphoid tissue of the thymus, Hassall's corpuscles are still present in the medulla.
Thymus cells:
-epithelial cells.
-macrophages.
-dendritic cells.
-T lymphocytes.
In mo we observe:
A thymic framework formed by epithelial cells with a reticular appearance (stellate) forming the thymic reticulum more apparent in the medulla.
_These cells are irregularly shaped and stellate with a rounded, bulky and nucleolated nucleus.
Some of the extensions are joined to those of neighboring cells by desmosomes
-Others form pockets surrounding clusters of lymphocytes, hence the term: “nurse cell”.
-These cells are arranged in the medulla in an onion bulb: HASSAL corpuscle (globular cell clusters representing the final stage of evolution of reticular cells.
-Macrophages:
located in the subcapsular cortex
Ensure phagocytosis of lymphocytes dead by apoptosis
Dendritic cells
of monocytoid origin found throughout the thymic parenchyma
Role presenters of ATG.
Reticular cells,
Possess grains of secretions at the origin of thymic hormones which play an important role in the maturation of lymphocytes.
-T lymphocytes:
-Proliferation of lymphocytes or thymoblast: large blast cells in division attached to the plasma membrane of the reticulo-epithelial feeding cells
-maturation and differentiation of thymocytes appearance of CD4 CD8 receptors
-Migration towards the corticomedullary junction
-Differentiation at the level of the medulla. The lympho become CD4 or CD8 and are in contact with macrophages, dendritic cells and epithelial cells.
-Passage of thymocytes into the circulation.
The HASSAL corpuscle
Is formed from the periphery towards the center by cells which degenerate in 3 stages:
-nucleated scaly cells.
-flattened cells with pyknotic nucleus.
-keratinized cells.
The center of the corpuscle is occupied by granular cellular debris
-it is considered the family vault of the cells of the frame.
Thymus (medullary)
Medullary in MO at high magnification stained by HE
Hassal corpuscle: is a keratinizing differentiation of epithelial cells (production of
lymphopoietin, cemetery of epitheliocytes)
Histophysiology
-the thymus ensures lymphopoiesis of T cells.
-the epithelial reticular cells of the thymic framework provide 3 essential functions:
-support for the thymic parenchyma.

-secretion of several hormonal factors acting on lymphopoiesis including lymphopoietin which induces the differentiation of parent cells into T lymphocytes or thymocytes and the maturation of the latter into immunologically competent cells.
-direct role in immunity (rejection of transplants).
-indirect role in humoral immunity (cooperation with B lymphocytes)
-In the absence of ATG, T lymphocytes are at rest and have a short lifespan
○ auxiliaries or CD4 which promote the humoral response by stimulating the B
○ cytotoxic (CD8): kill tumor or infected cells
○ suppressors (CD8): inhibit the humoral response
○ NK (Natural Killer) cells
○ Secrete cytokines
○ Express an antigen receptor

The thymus connected to the vascular compartment receives stem cells which will differentiate into T precursors and proliferate. The thymus also serves to “train” newly formed LT and to recognize histo-accounting genes: “self” genes.
conclusion
The thymus is made up of cells: lymphoid, epithelial, macrophage and dendritic cells allowing the maturation of thymocytes.
The function of the thymus is to ensure the development and maturation of T lymphocytes.
